title: Lowest-weight distribution presentation of the dual induced module
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $S$ be a semisimple simply connected $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]: smooth, connected, affine and of finite type, with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, and with every surjective homomorphism from a semisimple group with finite central kernel an isomorphism. Solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial; finite central means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and commuting after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq B\subseteq S$ and a Borel subgroup $B$ with unipotent radical $U$, projection $\pi_T:B	o T$, character lattice $X=X^*(T)$, positive roots $\Phi^+$ in $\operatorname{Lie}(B)$, simple roots $\Delta$, and coroot pairing as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. A split torus is a product of copies of $\mathbf G_m$; a Borel is a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup; the unipotent radical is the largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup, where unipotent means unipotent geometric matrices in a faithful representation. Choose root parametrizations $x_i:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_{\alpha_i}$ for $\alpha_i\in\Delta$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Put $\epsilon:F[U]	o F$, evaluation at the identity, and $\mathfrak m=\ker\epsilon$. Define the distribution algebra $H=\operatorname{Dist}(U)= igcup_{r\geq0}\operatorname{Hom}_F(F[U]/\mathfrak m^{r+1},F)$, with product $(ab)(f)=(a\otimes b)(\Delta_U f)$, where $\Delta_U$ is induced by multiplication in $U$. Its unit is $\epsilon$. Let $D_i^{(n)}\in H$ be $f\mapsto[t^n]x_i^*f$ for $n\geq0$. A rational module means a vector space with a coassociative counital coordinate-algebra coaction $c$; a distribution $a$ acts by $(1\otimes a)c$. Let $w_0$ be the longest Weyl element [lem-sfb-rho-regular-weyl-orbit], and let $\eta\in X$ be any dominant character, meaning $m_i=\langle\eta,\alpha_i^\veeangle\geq0$. Put $Q=S/B$ and $M_\mu=\mathcal L_{-\mu\circ\pi_T}$, with quotient action $(g,z)\cdot b=(gb,\mu(\pi_T(b))z)$ [lem-sfb-homogeneous-line-bundle-sections]. Equip $V_\eta=\Gamma(Q,M_{-w_0\eta})$ with left translation. Then $V_\eta$ is nonzero and finite-dimensional. Its contragredient $W_\eta=\operatorname{Hom}_F(V_\eta,F)$, with $(g\ell)(v)=\ell(g^{-1}v)$ after every scalar extension, contains a nonzero vector $w$ of $T$-weight $-\eta$ such that
$$W_\eta=H w,\qquad D_i^{(n)}w=0\quad	ext{for every }i	ext{ and }n>m_i.$$
Here $Hw$ denotes the linear span of $aw$ for $a\in H$, and a $T$-weight $
u$ means $tw=
u(t)w$ after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. There is no restriction $m_i<p$ in this statement. For $S=1$, the assertions mean $V_0=W_0=F$, $H=F$, and $w
e0$.

proof.text: Put $\mu=-w_0\eta$. The map $-w_0$ permutes the simple roots: it and its inverse preserve the positive root cone, so they permute its indecomposable positive roots. Coroots transform compatibly by the rank-one reflection result. Thus $\mu$ is dominant. The simply connected lattice result writes $\mu=\sum_j a_j\omega_j$ with $a_j=\langle\mu,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle\geq0$. Choose $n_0$ representing $w_0$. The fundamental boundary sections $s_j$ are nonzero at $n_0B$, because each of their zero loci lies outside the open cell. In the regular-function identification for homogeneous line sections, let $f_j\in F[S]$ correspond to $s_j$; then $f_j(gb)=\omega_j(\pi_T(b))f_j(g)$ and $f_j(n_0)\ne0$. Their product $f=\prod_j f_j^{a_j}$ satisfies $f(gb)=\mu(\pi_T(b))f(g)$ and $f(n_0)\ne0$. The same identification therefore gives a section of $M_\mu$ nonzero at $n_0B$. Empty products are $1$.

source.place: 22.8--22.11 and 22.22--22.27, pp.464--470; 22.49, p.480. Geometric nonvanishing via the already stated fundamental boundary sections; signs follow the quotient action, not the conflicting dominance wording in 22.48.

proof.text: The Borel-pair statement makes $Q=S/B$ proper over $F$, and the homogeneous-line statement makes $M_\mu$ coherent. A field is Noetherian. Apply finite coherent cohomology with base $\operatorname{Spec}F$, $i=0$, to conclude that $V_\eta=\Gamma(Q,M_\mu)$ is finite-dimensional. It is nonzero by step 1. The equivariant regular-function identification realizes it as the left-translation space $E(-\mu\circ\pi_T)\subset F[S]$; this is its rational action. The finite-dimensional dual therefore has the contragredient rational action specified in the item (transpose of the inverse action matrix).

source.place: Tag 02O6, lemma-proper-over-affine-cohomology-finite, with Milne 18c and 22.21 for the homogeneous bundle and left-translation action.

proof.text:
For $v\in V_\eta$ write $f_v\in F[S]$ for its semi-invariant function and define $w(v)=f_v(n_0)$. Step 1 shows $w\ne0$. For every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and $t\in T(A)$ the action formulas give
$$(tw)(v)=w(t^{-1}v)=f_v(tn_0)=\mu(n_0^{-1}tn_0)f_v(n_0)=(w_0\mu)(t)w(v)=(-\eta)(t)w(v).$$
Here the character is evaluated multiplicatively, and $w_0^2=1$. These are identities of regular functions, hence of coactions; they hold on arbitrary scalar-extended vectors as well. Thus this actual evaluation functional has the required character weight, with no replacement of a character by its differential.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 22.22, pp.468--469: the torus action on the open-cell function; direct dual evaluation calculation.

proof.text:
The Bruhat-chart statement identifies $U$ with $\mathbf A_F^N$ and $u\mapsto un_0B$ with a dense open of the integral $Q$. Choose affine coordinates $z_1,\ldots,z_N$ on $U$ with the identity at $0$ (translate any such coordinates by their values at the identity). The map $v\mapsto P_v$, $P_v(u)=f_v(un_0)$, takes values in $F[z_1,\ldots,z_N]$ and is injective: if $P_v=0$, then semi-invariance gives $f_v(un_0b)=0$; the dense open $Un_0B$ in the integral $S$ forces the regular function $f_v$ to vanish. Indeed restriction of a domain to any nonempty principal open is injective. Also
$$(uw)(v)=w(u^{-1}v)=f_v(un_0)=P_v(u).$$
Thus $P_v$ is exactly the matrix coefficient of $w$ on the dual module, rather than a different regular function with an unspecified action convention.

source.place: Theorems 21.73 and 21.84, pp.447--451; proof of Proposition 22.22, pp.468--469. Mathieu, proof of Lemma 2.1, printed p.154, uses the same dense-orbit restriction.

proof.text:
Suppose $v\in V_\eta$ annihilates $Hw$. For every multi-index $\beta$, coefficient extraction $a_\beta(P)=[z^\beta]P$ vanishes on $(z_1,\ldots,z_N)^{|\beta|+1}$, so $a_\beta\in H$ by the definition in the statement. Applying the distribution action to the matrix coefficient in step 4 gives
$$0=(a_\beta w)(v)=a_\beta(P_v)=[z^\beta]P_v.$$
All coefficients of the polynomial $P_v$ vanish, so $P_v=0$ and step 4 gives $v=0$. If $Hw$ were a proper subspace of the finite-dimensional $W_\eta=V_\eta^\vee$, extend a basis of $Hw$ to one of $W_\eta$ and take a nonzero coordinate functional killing $Hw$. Under the evaluation identification $V_\eta\cong W_\eta^\vee$ this would be a nonzero such $v$. This contradiction proves $Hw=W_\eta$. This argument uses coefficient distributions of every order; ordinary first derivatives would not suffice in characteristic $p$.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 2.3, printed p.155, cyclicity deduced from Lemma 2.1; agent-written explicit polynomial coefficient and finite-dimensional annihilator argument filling out that deduction.

proof.text:
Fix $i$, and write $\alpha_j=-w_0\alpha_i$, a simple root by step 1. The subgroup $n_0^{-1}U_{\alpha_i}n_0$ is smooth, connected, closed and normalized by $T$; for $t\in T(A)$, conjugation by $t$ scales its parameter by $\alpha_i(n_0tn_0^{-1})=(w_0\alpha_i)(t)=(-\alpha_j)(t)$, so its tangent space is $\mathfrak g_{-\alpha_j}$ and uniqueness of the root subgroup gives $n_0^{-1}U_{\alpha_i}n_0=U_{-\alpha_j}$. Let $\varphi:\operatorname{SL}_2\to S$ be the rank-one homomorphism of the opposite-root parametrization result for $\alpha_j$: $a\mapsto\varphi(I_2+aE_{12})$ and $a\mapsto\varphi(I_2+aE_{21})$ are isomorphisms of $\mathbf G_a$ onto $U_{\alpha_j}$ and $U_{-\alpha_j}$, and $\varphi(\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1}))=\alpha_j^\vee(s)$. Two isomorphisms $\mathbf G_a\to U_{-\alpha_j}$ differ by an automorphism of the affine line fixing $0$, which is $t\mapsto ct$; hence there is $c_i\in F^\times$ with
$$n_0^{-1}x_i(t)n_0=\varphi(I_2+c_itE_{21}).$$
The root-subgroup product result, applied with $B'=B$, gives $U_{\alpha_j}\subseteq U\subseteq B$, since $\alpha_j\in\Phi^+$. Every point of the upper triangular subgroup $B_2\subseteq\operatorname{SL}_2$ is $b=\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})(I_2+aE_{12})$, so $\varphi(B_2)\subseteq B$ and $\pi_T(\varphi(b))=\alpha_j^\vee(s)$, because $\pi_T$ is the identity on $T$ and has kernel $U$. We do not use the Schubert-curve homomorphism, whose statement does not say which subgroups its unipotent matrices map to.

source.place: 21.19 and 21.24, p.432 (the rank-one isogeny v_alpha restricts to isomorphisms U^+ -> U_alpha and U^- -> U_-alpha), and Lemma 21.28, p.433 (a Borel subgroup containing T contains U_alpha or U_-alpha); the normalizer calculation is written here.

proof.text:
Put $d=\langle\mu,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle$. Normalizer conjugation carries $\alpha_i^\vee$ to $(w_0\alpha_i)^\vee$ and preserves the pairing, and $(-\beta)^\vee=-\beta^\vee$ because both satisfy the reflection identity for $s_\beta=s_{-\beta}$ and that cocharacter is unique. Hence
$$d=\langle-w_0\eta,-w_0\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=m_i\geq0.$$
For $v\in V_\eta$ put $\psi(h)=f_v(n_0\varphi(h))$, a regular function on $\operatorname{SL}_2$. By step 6 and the semi-invariance of $f_v$, for $b=\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})(I_2+aE_{12})$ over any $A$ one has $\psi(hb)=\mu(\alpha_j^\vee(s))\psi(h)=s^d\psi(h)$. Let $g_x\in\operatorname{SL}_2$ have entries $(g_x)_{11}=x$, $(g_x)_{12}=-1$, $(g_x)_{21}=1$, $(g_x)_{22}=0$, and put $P(z)=\psi(I_2+zE_{21})\in F[z]$, $R(x)=\psi(g_x)\in F[x]$. Over $A=F[z,z^{-1}]$, multiplying out gives
$$I_2+zE_{21}=g_{z^{-1}}\operatorname{diag}(z,z^{-1})(I_2+z^{-1}E_{12}),$$
so $P(z)=z^dR(z^{-1})$ in $F[z,z^{-1}]$. The right side has no monomial of degree above $d$, hence $\deg P\leq m_i$. By step 6, $f_v(x_i(t)n_0)=f_v(n_0\varphi(I_2+c_itE_{21}))=P(c_it)$ also has degree at most $m_i$ in $t$. Taking its $t^n$ coefficient in the matrix coefficient of step 4 gives
$$(D_i^{(n)}w)(v)=[t^n]f_v(x_i(t)n_0)=0\quad(n>m_i).$$
All $v$ vanish on this vector, so $D_i^{(n)}w=0$. No factorial was divided by and no hypothesis $m_i<p$ was used.

source.place: 21.24, p.432, and the proof of Proposition 22.22, pp.468--469 (restriction of open-cell functions to root groups); the SL_2 factorization and degree bound are agent-written.

proof.text: For $S=1$, the character lattice is zero, $\eta=0$, $Q=\operatorname{Spec}F$, and the homogeneous bundle is the trivial line. Hence $V_0=W_0=F$, the coordinate ring of $U=1$ is $F$ with augmentation ideal zero, and $H=F$. Evaluation is $w=1$ and generates $F$; there are no simple-root relations to check. For any $S$, $\eta=0$ also causes no problem: step 1 uses an empty product and step 7 gives degree zero on each root curve.
